paras: The Abbeville regulator whippings and expulsions were a series of night whippings and armed expulsion orders at Abbeville, in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana, in August 1888, carried out first by a party of young men called "regulators" and then by a mounted citizens' committee. When the regulators went to the house of a Black man named Shepard, who was living with a white woman, a shotgun fired from the house wounded one of them. Wire reports first framed it as a clash over "miscegenation" and later as a biracial campaign against "bad characters," whose exiles were tied to a deadly fight at Freetown.

In early August the Abbeville Meridional reported "daily rumors" of regulators "soundly whipping all violators of well established social and moral obligations" in nearby parishes, and feared "some one will get hurt." The regulators, "or Caucasians as they are called," had warned white men living with Black women, and the reverse, to leave the parish, a New Orleans dispatch said. A Picayune correspondent at Lafayette described Abbeville as "infested with bad men and women" who flouted local proprieties.

On a Saturday night, which by the dates of the dispatches was August 11, a party of young men, mostly store clerks, began whipping several men and women with cowhides or switches. In their rounds they demanded admittance at the house of a white woman living with Shepard, "a negro" in the Sun and "a mulatto" in a later dispatch. According to T. D. Foster of New Iberia, the party meant to switch the man, and the woman fired a shotgun into the crowd. The wounded man was named as John Abadle, John A. Badie or Jno. A. Bodie, and the regulators withdrew.

On Monday a call went out for an indignation meeting, which met the next day with about 400 people, one-third of them "colored," according to the dispatch. Its resolutions condemned "the women and vagrants whose open immorality inspired the meeting" and ordered them to leave the community. That evening about 100 armed, mounted committeemen, white and Black, gave those named twelve hours to leave, and the committee rode again on Wednesday. The dispatch said the committee whipped only one person, a white man.

The Attakapas Rangers of Iberia were summoned to arms, and Foster said New Iberia citizens stood ready to help "the Abbeville people." By August 16, however, New Orleans heard that the excitement was subsiding, the militia had been dismissed and the wounded man was recovering. The governor sent Captain Taylor Cade of the Iberia Guards to investigate, and the sheriff told him the community could take care of itself.

Most of those ordered away left and gathered at a point between New Iberia and Lafayette. Exiles were reported at Freetown, a Black village near New Iberia, where civil engineer E. P. Smith was killed in a clash on August 16. The Indianapolis Journal reported nineteen Black residents missing there, and an August 18 dispatch said more than twenty had been killed. No report of arrests or charges over the Abbeville whippings or the shooting appears in the coverage.

The first New Orleans wire, printed in the New York Sun on August 17 under the headline "OPPOSED TO MISCEGENATION," presented the raids as an attempt to "break up miscegenation" and noted that a meeting had "endorsed the action of the regulators." Reprints followed as "A Fatal Encounter" in Wheeling and "RAIDED BY REGULATORS" in St. Paul. The New-York Tribune's special was headed "A 'REGULATOR' SHOT BY A WOMAN."

The August 18 dispatch reversed that emphasis, opening "No race issue is involved in the trouble at Abbeville." The Memphis Appeal headed it "NO RACE TROUBLE," and Kansas weeklies reprinted it as "A War on Bad Characters" and "NO RACE ISSUE INVOLVED." The Tribune ran the same text without that line, under "AS USUAL, NEGROES WERE THE ONES KILLED." No account quoted Shepard, the woman or anyone ordered to leave.

Most reports said the woman fired; the Indianapolis Journal said "the negro shot one of the regulators." The Sun called the wound fatal, but later reports had the man slightly hurt or recovering. The raid is dated Saturday night in most accounts, Friday or Tuesday in others, and one report gave the committee as twelve men.

reader.title: Abbeville regulator whippings and expulsions
bases: A night band of 'regulators' whipped men and women it accused of immorality and warned interracial couples to leave the parish, and a mass meeting's armed committee then ordered 'bad characters' out in twelve hours (A4, A11, A12).

The New Orleans wire (A4), T. D. Foster's interview (A2), the Picayune's Lafayette special (A15) and the Aug. 18 dispatch (A11, A12) independently report the whippings and the shot fired from the house at the regulators, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire (Aug. 16-17)
accounts.gist: Regulators, 'or Caucasians,' warned interracial couples to leave Vermilion, whipped a white man on Tuesday, and at Shepard's house the woman fired a shotgun, fatally wounding one; a meeting endorsed the regulators.

accounts.label: T. D. Foster of New Iberia
accounts.gist: Regulators went to switch a Black man living with a white woman; she fired into the crowd, badly wounding a young man; Black residents were said to be arming. A later note said the wounded man was recovering.

accounts.label: Picayune special from Lafayette / Aug. 18 dispatch
accounts.gist: Young men, mostly clerks, whipped several men and women on Saturday night; someone in a white woman's house fired, wounding one; an interracial meeting ordered 'bad characters' out and an armed committee enforced it; 'No race issue is involved.'

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal special
accounts.gist: Regulators whipped a white woman and a Black man on Friday; the man shot a regulator, and disreputable Black residents were driven to Freetown.

framing.detail: The Sun's 'OPPOSED TO MISCEGENATION' and the Wheeling and St. Paul reprints described the regulators' aim and the 'fatal encounter' without comment.
The Aug. 18 dispatch ('NO RACE TROUBLE' in Memphis, 'A War on Bad Characters' in Kansas) presented the expulsions as a biracial 'demonstration of public sentiment' against 'bad characters'.
The New-York Tribune ran the same Aug. 18 text under 'AS USUAL, NEGROES WERE THE ONES KILLED,' leading with the Freetown deaths.
The Abbeville Meridional said the regulators' whippings would 'doubtless accomplish much good' while fearing someone would get hurt.

conflicts.note: Most accounts name the woman; only the Indianapolis special says the man fired.

versions.value: badly wounding, almost sure to die, later recovering

conflicts.note: The later dispatches (Aug. 16 note and Aug. 18) describe recovery or a slight wound; no death is reported.
Saturday night is the date in the most detailed and the local-correspondent accounts; Tuesday matches the date of the indignation meeting in the Aug. 18 dispatch.
